questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (functional group) with List-II (example given in NCERT).

List-I:
A. Herbivores of terrestrial ecosystems
B. Herbivores of aquatic ecosystems
C. Producers of aquatic ecosystems
D. Decomposers

List-II:
I. Molluscs
II. Fungi and bacteria
III. Insects, birds and mammals
IV. Phytoplankton, some algae and higher plants

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II
A-I, B-III, C-IV, D-II
A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV
A-IV, B-I, C-III, D-II

solution.concept: Members of the functional groups of ecosystems
solution.explanation: NCERT: the common herbivores are insects, birds and mammals in terrestrial ecosystems and molluscs in aquatic ecosystems. In aquatic ecosystems the primary producers are phytoplankton, some algae and higher plants. Decomposers are heterotrophic organisms, mainly fungi and bacteria.
steps: Aquatic producers: phytoplankton, some algae, higher plants
solution.why_others_wrong: Option B swaps the terrestrial and aquatic herbivores; option C swaps producers and decomposers; option D gives the producers to the terrestrial herbivores.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', ecosystem - structure and function; energy flow
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: According to NCERT, the basic requirement for any ecosystem to function and sustain itself is:

options.text: A constant input of chemical fertilisers
The absence of decomposers
An inverted pyramid of biomass
A constant input of solar energy

solution.concept: Solar energy as the driving input
solution.explanation: NCERT opens the section on productivity by stating that a constant input of solar energy is the basic requirement for any ecosystem to function and sustain. Plants convert part of this energy into organic matter (primary production).
steps: Constant solar input → primary production → rest of the ecosystem
solution.why_others_wrong: Fertilisers are not a basic requirement of natural ecosystems; decomposers are essential; pyramids describe structure and are not a requirement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', productivity
solution.final_answer: Option D: A constant input of solar energy

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Decomposers secrete digestive enzymes that break down dead and waste materials into simple inorganic materials, which they then absorb. Decomposers are therefore also known as:

options.text: Autotrophs
Producers
Saprotrophs
Herbivores

solution.explanation: NCERT: decomposers are also known as saprotrophs (sapro: to decompose). They secrete digestive enzymes that break down dead and waste materials into simple inorganic materials, which are subsequently absorbed by them.
solution.why_others_wrong: Autotrophs and producers make their own food; herbivores feed on living plants.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', energy flow
solution.final_answer: Option C: Saprotrophs

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: According to NCERT, the energy trapped by a producer is either passed on to a consumer or:

options.text: It is returned to the sun as reflected light
The organism dies, and its death is the beginning of the detritus food chain/web
It is stored permanently in the producer and never released
It is recycled back to the same producer by herbivores

solution.concept: Fate of energy fixed by producers
solution.explanation: NCERT: the energy trapped by the producer is either passed on to a consumer or the organism dies. Death of the organism is the beginning of the detritus food chain/web, through which decomposers obtain energy.
steps: Producer dies → detritus food chain/web begins
solution.why_others_wrong: Energy flow is unidirectional and is not returned to the sun or recycled to the producer; stored energy is released when the producer is eaten or decomposed.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', energy flow
solution.final_answer: Option B: The organism dies, and its death is the beginning of the detritus food chain/web

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The interaction of biotic and abiotic components results in a physical structure that is characteristic of each type of ecosystem.
Statement II: Primary productivity is the same in all ecosystems, because it does not depend on the plant species or on environmental factors.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Structure of ecosystems; factors affecting productivity
solution.explanation: NCERT: interaction of biotic and abiotic components results in a physical structure characteristic of each type of ecosystem (Statement I true). Primary productivity depends on the plant species inhabiting an area and on environmental factors, the availability of nutrients and the photosynthetic capacity of plants, so it varies in different types of ecosystems (Statement II false).
steps: Statement II: false, productivity varies between ecosystems
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', ecosystem - structure and function; productivity
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about ecological pyramids are correct?

(a) In a pyramid of energy, the bar for the producers is the widest.
(b) In the pyramid of biomass of a sea, the bar for the phytoplankton is narrower than the bar for the fishes.
(c) A pyramid of energy becomes inverted when the producers are small in size.
(d) In a grassland, the pyramid of numbers is narrowest at the level of the top carnivores.
(e) The apex of an ecological pyramid is formed by the decomposers.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: (a), (b) and (d) only
(a), (c) and (d) only
(b), (c) and (e) only
(a), (d) and (e) only

solution.explanation: Energy is always lost as heat at each step, so the producer bar of the energy pyramid is always the widest and the pyramid can never be inverted. In the sea, the biomass of fishes far exceeds that of phytoplankton, so the biomass pyramid is inverted (narrow producer bar). In a grassland, producers far outnumber herbivores, which outnumber carnivores, so the top carnivores form the narrow apex. Decomposers (saprophytes) are not given any place in ecological pyramids.
steps: (c): false, the energy pyramid is never inverted
(e): false, saprophytes have no place in pyramids
solution.why_others_wrong: Options B, C and D each include (c) or (e).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', ecological pyramids
solution.final_answer: Option A: (a), (b) and (d) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The net primary productivity of an ecosystem is always less than its gross primary productivity.
Reason (R): A considerable amount of gross primary productivity is utilised by plants in respiration.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Gross primary productivity is the rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis. A considerable part of it is used by the plants in respiration (R), and NPP = GPP − R. Because R is always subtracted, NPP is less than GPP; R is the direct reason.
steps: NPP = GPP − R → R explains A
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', productivity
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Like its pyramid of biomass, the pyramid of energy of a sea is inverted.
Reason (R): In a sea, the biomass of fishes far exceeds that of the phytoplankton.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Inverted biomass pyramid versus upright energy pyramid
solution.explanation: The pyramid of biomass in a sea is generally inverted because the biomass of fishes far exceeds that of the phytoplankton, so R is true. The pyramid of energy, however, is always upright and can never be inverted, because energy is lost as heat at every step from one trophic level to the next. So A is false.
steps: A: false, energy pyramids are always upright
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', ecological pyramids
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: In an ecosystem, the energy present at successive trophic levels is: producers 8,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹, herbivores 640 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ and primary carnivores 64 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹. What percentage of energy is transferred from producers to herbivores, and from herbivores to primary carnivores, respectively?

options.text: 10 per cent and 8 per cent
12.5 per cent and 10 per cent
8 per cent and 10 per cent
92 per cent and 90 per cent

solution.concept: Efficiency of energy transfer between trophic levels
solution.explanation: Transfer efficiency = energy at the higher level ÷ energy at the lower level × 100. Producers → herbivores: 640/8000 × 100 = 8 per cent. Herbivores → carnivores: 64/640 × 100 = 10 per cent. NCERT's 10 per cent law is an approximation; the rest of the energy is lost, mostly as heat.
solution.why_others_wrong: Option A reverses the order; 12.5 is the inverted ratio 8000/640 (not a percentage); 92 and 90 per cent are the fractions not transferred.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', energy flow; ecological pyramids
solution.final_answer: Option C: 8 per cent and 10 per cent

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Decomposers are heterotrophic organisms.
Reason (R): Humus is highly resistant to microbial action and undergoes decomposition at an extremely slow rate.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Decomposers, mainly fungi and bacteria, are heterotrophs that meet their energy and nutrient requirements by degrading dead organic matter, so A is true. Humus is highly resistant to microbial action and decomposes extremely slowly, so R is true. R describes a property of humus and does not explain why decomposers are heterotrophic.
steps: R concerns humus, not the nutrition of decomposers
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', energy flow; decomposition
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In NCERT's pyramid of numbers for a grassland ecosystem, the top carnivores are the fewest in number.
Reason (R): Top carnivores capture the largest share of the energy that flows through the ecosystem.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Numbers and energy at the top of the food chain
solution.explanation: In the grassland pyramid of numbers, producers far outnumber herbivores, herbivores outnumber carnivores, and the top carnivores are the fewest, so A is true. Energy decreases at each successive trophic level because energy is lost as heat at every transfer, so the top carnivores receive the smallest share of energy, not the largest; R is false.
steps: R: false, the top level receives the least energy
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Ecosystem', ecological pyramids; energy flow
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: The term 'biodiversity', popularised by the sociobiologist Edward Wilson, describes:

options.text: Only the number of species found in a region
Only the genetic variation within a single species
The combined diversity at all the levels of biological organisation
Only the variety of ecosystems in a country

solution.explanation: NCERT: biodiversity is the term popularised by Edward Wilson to describe the combined diversity at all the levels of biological organisation. The most important of these are genetic diversity, species diversity and ecological diversity.
steps: Biodiversity = combined diversity at all levels of biological organisation
solution.why_others_wrong: Species richness, genetic variation and ecosystem variety are each only one level of biodiversity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', biodiversity
solution.final_answer: Option C: The combined diversity at all the levels of biological organisation

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Besides finding that plots with more species showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass, David Tilman's outdoor-plot experiments showed that increased diversity contributed to:

options.text: Lower productivity
Higher productivity
Greater invasion by alien species
More frequent pest outbreaks

solution.explanation: Tilman's long-term ecosystem experiments with outdoor plots found that plots with more species showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass, and that increased diversity contributed to higher productivity.
solution.why_others_wrong: Tilman's results showed the opposite of lower productivity; NCERT links stable, species-rich communities with resistance to invasions and less variability in pest cycles.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', biodiversity: importance of species diversity to the ecosystem
solution.final_answer: Option B: Higher productivity

questions.subject: Botany
questions.subtopic: In situ and ex situ conservation
questions.question_text: Besides the Khasi and Jaintia Hills of Meghalaya, NCERT lists sacred groves in:

options.text: The Thar desert of Rajasthan and the Rann of Kutch in Gujarat
The Sundarbans of West Bengal and the Andaman Islands
The Deccan plateau of Telangana and the coastal plains of Odisha
The Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan, the Western Ghat regions of Karnataka and Maharashtra, and the Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas of Madhya Pradesh

solution.explanation: In India, ecologically unique and biodiversity-rich regions are legally protected, and many cultures also set aside tracts of forest as sacred groves. NCERT: such sacred groves are found in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills in Meghalaya, the Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan, the Western Ghat regions of Karnataka and Maharashtra and the Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas of Madhya Pradesh.
steps: Sacred grove regions: Khasi-Jaintia Hills, Aravalli Hills, Western Ghats (Karnataka, Maharashtra), Sarguja-Chanda-Bastar (MP)
solution.why_others_wrong: None of the regions in the other options is listed by NCERT as a location of sacred groves.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', biodiversity conservation: in situ conservation
solution.final_answer: Option D: The Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan, the Western Ghat regions of Karnataka and Maharashtra, and the Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas of Madhya Pradesh

questions.subject: Botany
questions.subtopic: In situ and ex situ conservation
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In Meghalaya, the sacred groves are the last refuges for a large number of rare and threatened plants.
Reason (R): The last twenty years alone have witnessed the disappearance of 27 species.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: in Meghalaya, the sacred groves are the last refuges for a large number of rare and threatened plants (A true). In discussing the loss of biodiversity, NCERT notes that the last twenty years alone have witnessed the disappearance of 27 species (R true). R is a general statement about recent extinctions and does not explain why the sacred groves of Meghalaya shelter rare plants (their total protection does).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', biodiversity conservation: in situ conservation; loss of biodiversity
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.subtopic: In situ and ex situ conservation
questions.question_text: Seeds of different genetic strains of commercially important plants can be kept for long periods in:

options.text: Seed banks
Sacred groves
Biosphere reserves
National parks

solution.concept: Seed banks as ex situ conservation
solution.explanation: Ex situ conservation now uses advanced techniques: gametes of threatened species can be cryopreserved, eggs fertilised in vitro and plants propagated by tissue culture. NCERT adds that seeds of different genetic strains of commercially important plants can be kept for long periods in seed banks.
steps: Long-term storage of seeds of genetic strains: seed banks (ex situ)
solution.why_others_wrong: Sacred groves, biosphere reserves and national parks are in situ methods that protect living plants in their habitat; they do not store seeds.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', biodiversity conservation: ex situ conservation
solution.final_answer: Option A: Seed banks

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (scientist) with List-II (contribution described in NCERT).

List-I:
A. Edward Wilson
B. Robert May
C. Paul Ehrlich
D. David Tilman

List-II:
I. 'Rivet popper' hypothesis
II. Long-term ecosystem experiments using outdoor plots
III. Estimate of global species diversity at about 7 million
IV. Popularised the term 'biodiversity'

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I
A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II
A-I, B-III, C-IV, D-II
A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II

solution.concept: Scientists in the study of biodiversity
solution.explanation: Edward Wilson popularised the term biodiversity; Robert May placed the global species diversity at about 7 million; Paul Ehrlich proposed the 'rivet popper' hypothesis comparing species to the rivets of an airplane; and David Tilman carried out long-term ecosystem experiments using outdoor plots.
solution.why_others_wrong: Option A swaps Ehrlich and Tilman; option B swaps Wilson and May; option C swaps Wilson and Ehrlich.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', biodiversity; importance of species diversity to the ecosystem
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The diversity of plants and animals is not uniform throughout the world but shows a rather uneven distribution.
Statement II: In general, species diversity increases as we move away from the equator towards the poles.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: the diversity of plants and animals is not uniform throughout the world but shows a rather uneven distribution (Statement I true). The best-known pattern is the latitudinal gradient: species diversity decreases as we move away from the equator towards the poles, so Statement II is false.
steps: Statement II: false, diversity decreases towards the poles
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', patterns of biodiversity: latitudinal gradients
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When species richness is plotted against area on ordinary (linear) axes, the species-area relationship is a straight line.
Reason (R): On a logarithmic scale, the species-area relationship is a straight line described by log S = log C + Z log A.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Within a region, species richness increases with explored area, but only up to a limit; on linear axes the relation turns out to be a rectangular hyperbola, so A is false. On a logarithmic scale it is a straight line, log S = log C + Z log A, so R is true.
steps: A: false, it is a rectangular hyperbola
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', patterns of biodiversity: species-area relationships
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.subtopic: In situ and ex situ conservation
questions.question_text: To save a threatened orchid, a state government plans to: (i) declare its forest habitat a national park; (ii) store its seeds in a seed bank; (iii) grow it in a botanical garden; (iv) propagate it by tissue culture. Which of these are means of ex situ conservation?

options.text: (i) and (iii) only
(ii), (iii) and (iv) only
(i), (ii) and (iv) only
(i), (ii), (iii) and (iv)

solution.explanation: In situ conservation protects species in their natural habitat (national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, sacred groves). Ex situ conservation takes threatened species out of their natural habitat into special settings: botanical gardens, zoological parks, wildlife safari parks, seed banks, cryopreservation, in vitro fertilisation and tissue culture. So (ii), (iii) and (iv) are ex situ; (i) is in situ.
steps: (ii) seed bank, (iii) botanical garden, (iv) tissue culture: ex situ
solution.why_others_wrong: Every other option includes the national park (in situ) or leaves out an ex situ measure.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', biodiversity conservation: in situ and ex situ conservation
solution.final_answer: Option B: (ii), (iii) and (iv) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For frugivorous (fruit-eating) birds and mammals in the tropical forests of different continents, the slope Z of the species-area regression line is found to be 1.15.
Statement II: For areas within a region, the value of Z lies in the range 0.6 to 1.2.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Values of Z in the species-area relationship
solution.explanation: NCERT: within a region, Z values are amazingly similar, in the range 0.1 to 0.2, regardless of the taxonomic group or the region, so Statement II is false. When very large areas such as entire continents are analysed, the slope is much steeper (0.6 to 1.2); for frugivorous birds and mammals in the tropical forests of different continents, it is 1.15 (Statement I true).
steps: Statement II: false, within a region Z = 0.1 to 0.2
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', patterns of biodiversity: species-area relationships
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Species richness and area follow log S = log C + Z log A. Two very large areas, one 1000 times larger than the other, are compared, and the larger area has 100 times as many species. What is Z, and how does it compare with the ranges given in NCERT?

options.text: Z ≈ 0.67, within the range found for very large areas such as entire continents
Z = 1.5, steeper than any range given in NCERT
Z = 0.1, the value typical of areas within a region
Z ≈ 0.67, the value typical of areas within a region

solution.explanation: Subtracting the equations for the two areas: log(S₂/S₁) = Z log(A₂/A₁). So log 100 = Z × log 1000, i.e. 2 = 3Z and Z = 2/3 ≈ 0.67. NCERT: Z is 0.1-0.2 for areas within a region but much steeper, 0.6-1.2, for very large areas such as entire continents; 0.67 falls in the second range.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.5 inverts the logarithms (3/2); 0.1 divides the ratios themselves (100/1000) instead of their logarithms; 0.67 is outside the within-region range of 0.1-0.2.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Biology, 'Biodiversity and Conservation', patterns of biodiversity: species-area relationships
solution.final_answer: Option A: Z ≈ 0.67, within the range found for very large areas such as entire continents
